ai.definition: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) are a theoretical framework that combines principles of quantum computing with artificial neural networks to potentially process and learn from vast amounts of data more efficiently than classical systems.
ai.howItWorks: QNNs utilize the superposition and entanglement properties of qubits, allowing them to represent multiple states simultaneously. This enables parallel processing on a scale not achievable by classical computers, which can significantly speed up learning processes in machine learning tasks.
ai.problemSolved: Current limitations in classical computing for handling large datasets and complex models, leading to slow training times and high computational costs.
ai.manufacturing: Theoretical; no practical manufacturing process exists yet due to the immature state of quantum hardware technology.
ai.buildProcess: Requires development of quantum algorithms tailored for neural network architectures, which is currently a research challenge. Also involves creating qubits with sufficient coherence time and error correction capabilities.
ai.costDrivers: High development costs in quantum computing infrastructure, specialized talent required for both quantum and machine learning expertise, and the need for significant computational resources during training phases.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term potential but currently facing technical and practical challenges that limit its widespread adoption.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations yet due to early stage of development. However, as it matures, regulatory frameworks for quantum computing will likely evolve.
ai.risks: Technological uncertainties, high initial investment costs, and the risk of quantum decoherence during operations.
ai.profitability: Uncertain; currently a research field with no commercial applications yet.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential advancements in quantum hardware technology could enable practical QNN implementations. However, significant breakthroughs are needed to make them viable for real-world problems.

glossary.def: A type of computing that uses quantum bits (qubits) and quantum mechanics principles, allowing for parallel processing and solving certain problems much faster than classical computers.
The ability of a qubit to exist in multiple states simultaneously until measured, enabling exponential computational power compared to binary systems.
A phenomenon where the quantum state of two or more particles is linked together such that the state of one cannot be described independently of the others.

subsystems.name: Quantum processor
subsystems.role: holds and manipulates the qubits that do the computation.
parts: physical qubits (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic or neutral-atom)

subsystems.name: Data encoder
subsystems.role: loads classical data into quantum states as an input state or feature map.

subsystems.name: Parameterized circuit (ansatz)
subsystems.role: the trainable part — a repeating pattern of gates whose angles are the weights being learned.

subsystems.name: Measurement and readout
subsystems.role: extracts numbers from the quantum state by repeating the run many times (shots).

subsystems.name: Classical optimizer
subsystems.role: updates the circuit parameters to reduce the loss.

subsystems.name: Error mitigation and correction
subsystems.role: counters noise that corrupts results before it swamps the signal.

buildSteps.title: Choose the task and encoding
buildSteps.detail: A machine-learning problem is reduced to a form that can be loaded into qubits, usually as a feature map or a small data set.

buildSteps.title: Design the ansatz
buildSteps.detail: A layered circuit of rotation and entangling gates is chosen; its gate angles are the parameters to be trained.

buildSteps.title: Compile for the hardware
buildSteps.detail: The circuit is translated into the native gates and qubit connectivity of a specific device, adding swap operations where needed.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the machine
buildSteps.detail: Qubit frequencies, pulse amplitudes and readout thresholds are tuned before a run.

buildSteps.title: Execute and sample
buildSteps.detail: The circuit is run many times; each run ends in a measurement, and the average gives an estimate of an output value.

buildSteps.title: Update classically in a loop
buildSteps.detail: A classical computer estimates the gradient and adjusts the parameters, then the circuit is run again — often thousands of iterations.

buildSteps.title: Mitigate or correct errors
buildSteps.detail: Noise is measured and partly cancelled, or, in a fault-tolerant design, logical qubits are encoded so errors can be corrected mid-circuit.

buildSteps.title: Benchmark honestly
buildSteps.detail: The result must beat the best classical method on the same data at comparable cost; so far this has rarely happened.

buildSteps.title: Scale the qubit count
buildSteps.detail: Useful learning tasks would likely need many logical qubits and long coherence — beyond today's machines.

prerequisites.why: today's noisy qubits lose coherence within microseconds, so deep circuits cannot run reliably.
copying large classical data sets into a quantum state can cost more than the speed-up it might buy.
many ansatz designs have gradients that vanish as qubit count grows, making training impractical.

prerequisites.tech: Theory of quantum advantage for learning
prerequisites.why: proven speed-ups exist for narrow problems, but broad claims about machine learning remain unproven.
the baseline a quantum model must beat — GPUs and specialised chips are cheap, mature and improving fast.

pathway.milestone: small variational circuits run on noisy hardware in research labs, mostly matching or losing to classical models
pathway.unlocks: hands-on understanding of noise, encodings and optimisers.

pathway.milestone: demonstrated advantage on a narrow, well-defined learning task with a fair classical comparison
pathway.unlocks: a credible reason to keep building the field.

pathway.milestone: early error-corrected logical qubits running repeated circuits
pathway.unlocks: deeper ansatze and larger data sets without noise dominating.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant processors with thousands of logical qubits
pathway.unlocks: the possibility of genuine quantum machine learning — still unproven even then.
